story: Xuanzang recorded a reclining Buddha a thousand feet long sleeping somewhere beneath the valley — archaeologists still search for it; locals long called the standing pair Salsal and Shahmama, a petrified prince and princess of separated love.

name: Dhakeshwari National Temple
significance: The 'hidden goddess of Dhaka' who may have given the capital its name — since 1996 formally the National Temple of Bangladesh, centre of the country's Durga Puja and of Hindu public life. The original 800-year-old Dhakeshwari image was carried to Kolkata's Kumartuli in 1948, where it is still worshipped; the Dhaka shrine, damaged in 1971, was restored as the community's anchor.
story: Ballal Sena, the story runs, found an image of the goddess concealed (dhaka) in the jungle and enshrined her as Dhaka-Ishwari — the concealed sovereign lady from whom the megacity takes its name.

name: Kantajew Temple (Kantanagar)
significance: The finest terracotta temple of Bangladesh: every inch of its brick skin — some 15,000 plaques — narrates the epics, the Krishna lila, and the courtly life of 18th-century Bengal, from river barges to Portuguese muskets. Originally nine-spired, it lost its ratnas in the great 1897 earthquake yet remains the masterpiece of late Bengal temple art.
story: Its panels are read like a scroll by village storytellers at the Ras Mela — the annual fair when the deity travels by palanquin to Dinajpur town, a procession running unbroken since the Raj family's vow three centuries ago.

name: Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur
significance: The largest single Buddhist monastery south of the Himalaya — a quadrangle of 177 cells around a towering cruciform shrine whose terraced form, scholars argue, echoes across Bagan and even Angkor. A powerhouse of Pala-era learning tied to Nalanda and Vikramashila; the great teacher Atisha, who renewed Buddhism in Tibet, is associated with residence here. UNESCO-listed in 1985.
story: Its terracotta plaques mix Buddhas with snake-charmers, dancers and amorous couples — the monastery recording the whole world it renounced; Tibetan histories remember 'Somapuri' as one of the five jewel-viharas of the Pala realm.

name: Shwedagon Pagoda
deity: Relic stupa (eight hairs of the Buddha)
builtDisplay: raised to present form 14th–18th c.; origins far older
originNote: Mon foundations; legend places relics in the Buddha's lifetime
patron: Queen Shin Sawbu; King Dhammazedi; crown re-gilded by Mindon
significance: The golden heart of Myanmar: a 99 m stupa sheathed in genuine gold plates, its hti umbrella crusted with thousands of diamonds and rubies — enshrining, by tradition, eight hairs of the Buddha and relics of three predecessors, making it the oldest relic pagoda in Buddhist reckoning. Queen Shin Sawbu gave her weight in gold to gild it, beginning a national practice; every movement in Burmese history, royal or democratic, has rallied on this hill.
story: The merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika, first lay disciples, carried the Buddha's eight hairs home across the sea; opened on Singuttara hill, the casket blazed — the hairs rose, rays healing the blind and deaf, jewels raining — and the relics were sealed where the gods had kept the staff, water-filter and robe of three earlier Buddhas.
access: Yangon; four covered stairways & lifts; dress code, barefoot precinct.

name: Ananda Temple, Bagan
significance: The masterpiece among Bagan's 3,500+ monuments — a whitewashed Greek-cross temple crowned with a gilded sikhara, holding four 9.5 m standing Buddhas of the present aeon. The Kassapa image's smile changes with the viewer's distance — grave up close, radiant from afar. Restored with Indian ASI collaboration after the 2016 earthquake; Bagan entered the UNESCO list in 2019.
story: Eight monks from India described to Kyanzittha the Himalayan cave-temple of Nandamula; entranced, he built its likeness — then, the chronicle says, had the architect killed so it could never be duplicated: Bagan's dark parable of singular beauty.

name: Shwezigon Pagoda, Bagan
significance: The prototype of the Burmese stupa — the gilded bell whose form Shwedagon and a thousand others follow — built by Anawrahta, unifier of Burma and champion of Theravada. Crucially, he installed images of the 37 nats (spirits) here, absorbing the old animism into the new faith: the compact that still defines Burmese religion.
story: The site chose itself: a white elephant bearing the frontal-bone relic was set loose, and where it knelt the stupa rose — 'Shwezigon', golden hill of victory sand, where relic, kingship and the tamed nats met.

name: Mahamuni Buddha Temple
significance: Myanmar's most venerated image: the seated Mahamuni, carried over the mountains from Arakan (Mrauk-U) as war booty in 1785 — an act that still shapes Rakhine memory. Male devotees have applied so much gold leaf that the body lies under 15 cm of lumpy gold; each dawn a senior monk washes the image's face and brushes its teeth before crowds, the country's most intimate daily rite.
story: The Buddha himself, visiting Arakan, is said to have breathed life onto the casting — 'my brother' he called it, promising it would remain to represent him for five thousand years; only the face is left ungilded, kept mirror-bright by the morning ablutions.

name: Kyaiktiyo Pagoda (Golden Rock)
significance: A gilded granite boulder poised impossibly on the brow of a cliff, crowned by a 7.3 m stupa — one of Buddhism's three holiest sites in Myanmar with Shwedagon and Mahamuni. Pilgrims cross a bridge to press gold leaf onto the rock (men only may touch it); the boulder visibly rocks yet never falls.
story: The hermit Taik Tha kept a hair of the Buddha hidden in his own hair-knot for a lifetime, yielding it to the king only on condition it rest in a rock shaped like his head; Thagyamin, king of the gods, found this boulder on the ocean floor — the hair beneath it, they say, is all that keeps it from the abyss.

name: Wat Phra Kaew (Temple of the Emerald Buddha)
native: วัดพระแก้ว
significance: Thailand's palladium: the 66 cm jadeite Buddha, discovered in 1434 when lightning split a Chiang Rai stupa, travelled through Lampang, Chiang Mai and two centuries in Laos before Rama I enshrined it in his new Bangkok. The King of Thailand himself changes its gold seasonal robes thrice yearly; no other hand may touch it. The surrounding gallery holds the 178-panel Ramakien — Thailand's Ramayana — in mural form.
story: The image, legend claims, was fashioned in India by the gods' craftsman for the sage Nagasena, who prophesied it would carry Buddhism to five lands; wherever the Emerald Buddha resides, sovereignty and rain follow — which is why Laos and Siam contested it for centuries.
access: Grand Palace complex; strict dress code.

name: Wat Arun (Temple of Dawn)
builtDisplay: great prang raised under Rama II–III
significance: Bangkok's river icon: a 70–80 m Khmer-style prang sheathed in flowers of broken Chinese porcelain — ballast from trade junks turned to ornament — representing Mount Meru rising from the ocean. King Taksin reached this temple at dawn in 1767 after Ayutthaya's fall and made it home to the Emerald Buddha before Bangkok proper was founded across the river.
story: Named for Aruna, the Indian dawn-god and charioteer of the sun — the Hindu cosmos embedded in a Buddhist skyline; Indra on Erawan, the three-headed elephant, rides the prang's second terrace.

name: Wat Pho (Reclining Buddha)
significance: Bangkok's oldest and largest wat: the 46 m gold-leafed Reclining Buddha entering nirvana, feet inlaid with 108 mother-of-pearl auspicious signs. Rama III turned the cloisters into an open university — over a thousand inscriptions of medicine, massage and letters, now in UNESCO's Memory of the World — making Wat Pho the cradle of traditional Thai massage, still taught on site.
story: Dropping 108 coins in the 108 bronze bowls along the great image's back, pilgrims count off the Buddha's virtues — merit made audible, coin by coin, down the length of the sleeping giant.

name: Prasat Phanom Rung
significance: A Shaiva temple-mountain on the rim of an extinct volcano in Thailand's Khmer corridor, aligned so that at four moments a year the rising or setting sun pierces all fifteen doorways in a single shaft. The repatriation of its stolen Phra Narai (reclining Vishnu) lintel from the Art Institute of Chicago in 1988 became a national cause célèbre and a landmark of heritage return.
story: The sanctuary maps Shiva's Kailasa onto the volcano: the processional way crosses naga bridges — the passage from the human world across the cosmic ocean — before the mountain-summit sanctum where the hermit-prince Narendraditya retired as an ascetic.

name: Prasat Hin Phimai
significance: The largest Khmer temple in Thailand and terminus of the Ancient Khmer Highway from Angkor — 225 km of road, bridges and hospitals whose ceremonial gate faces Angkor itself. Built slightly before Angkor Wat, its central prang is widely seen as a design ancestor of that masterpiece; unusually for the empire, its heart is Tantric-Mahayana Buddhist.
story: Local legend weaves Phimai into the tale of Pachit and Oraphim — lovers whose trials named towns across the Khorat plateau; the temple's Buddhist dancer-lintels over Hindu doorframes record two faiths sharing one cosmology.

name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
significance: The mountain shrine of the North, its gilded chedi flashing over Chiang Mai from 1,000 m up Doi Suthep. Reached by a 306-step naga stairway; the road up was built in 1935 by tens of thousands of volunteers summoned by the charismatic monk Khruba Siwichai, finishing in under six months — northern Thailand's proudest act of collective merit.
story: A relic of the Buddha, brought north, miraculously doubled; one half was mounted on a white elephant let loose to choose its shrine — the beast climbed Doi Suthep, trumpeted three times, knelt and died: the chedi rose where it fell.

name: Angkor Wat
significance: The largest religious monument ever built — 162 hectares of moat, gallery and tower raised by Suryavarman II to Vishnu, its five peaks the mountain Meru, its bas-reliefs (including the 49 m Churning of the Ocean of Milk) the epics in stone. Uniquely west-facing; never wholly abandoned, it passed into Theravada worship and onto Cambodia's flag — the only building on any national flag. Angkor was UNESCO-listed in 1992 and is managed by the APSARA authority.
story: Khmer legend makes Angkor Wat the work of the divine architect Preah Pisnukar, built in a single night for the god-king; the moat is the cosmic ocean, and walking the west causeway at equinox one sees the sun rise exactly over the central tower — the universe re-centred each year.
access: Siem Reap ~6 km; Angkor Pass tickets; sunrise at the north pond is the classic darshan.

name: Bayon Temple, Angkor Thom
significance: State temple of Jayavarman VII, the empire's great Buddhist king — a forest of towers carved with over 200 colossal serene faces, compassion gazing to every horizon. Its outer galleries, uniquely, depict ordinary Khmer life — markets, cockfights, childbirth — beside the naval battle with the Chams that framed the king's rise.
story: The faces fuse Avalokiteshvara with Jayavarman himself — the bodhisattva-king watching all his people at once; stand anywhere in the Bayon and at least one face meets your eyes, the architectural claim that compassion has no blind spot.

name: Banteay Srei
significance: The 'Citadel of Women' — a miniature temple in rose-pink sandstone carved so deeply and finely it is called the jewel of Khmer art, and the rare great foundation built not by a king but by a scholar-priest, Yajnavaraha. Its pediments narrate Shiva's mythology with unmatched delicacy; the 1923 attempted theft of its apsaras by young André Malraux — future French culture minister — is one of art history's great scandals.
story: So fine is the carving that legend insisted no man's hand could have done it — the temple, people said, was carved by women; its guardian monkey-figures and the burning of Khandava forest pediment are keystones of Khmer myth in stone.

name: Ta Prohm
significance: The monastery Jayavarman VII dedicated to his mother as Prajnaparamita, goddess of wisdom — its stele records 12,640 residents and 66,000 farmers supporting it. Left deliberately in the forest's embrace by French conservators, its strangler figs and silk-cotton roots pouring over the galleries made it the world's image of ruin and return; India's ASI has partnered in its conservation since 2004.
story: The stele's inscription mourns and hopes at once: 'By the virtue of this good work, may my mother, freed from the ocean of existence, attain Buddhahood' — filial love as architecture, now cradled by the very jungle it once ordered.

name: Preah Vihear Temple
significance: Shiva as Lord of the Summit: an 800 m processional axis of stairways and gopuras climbing to a sanctuary on a 525 m Dangrek cliff over the Cambodian plain — the most dramatically sited of all Khmer temples. Awarded to Cambodia by the ICJ in 1962 (reaffirmed 2013) and UNESCO-listed in 2008, it remains entangled in recurring Thai–Cambodian border tensions — sacred geography as live geopolitics.
story: Legend ties the founding relic to a lock of Shiva's hair; the temple rises through five gopuras — pilgrims ascending, level by level, from the world of men to the god's mountain throne at the edge of the sky.

name: Sambor Prei Kuk (Ishanapura)
significance: Ishanapura, capital of Chenla — the temple city that came two centuries before Angkor, its brick sanctuaries (including unique octagonal towers) showing Indian temple ideas taking Khmer root. Here the flying-palace reliefs and inscribed Sanskrit foundations document Southeast Asia's creative absorption of the Indic world; UNESCO-listed in 2017.
story: Chinese envoys of the Sui court described Isanavarman's audience hall and five-day court cycle — the first outside portrait of a Khmer royal capital, matching the brick towers still standing in the 'forest of temples' (prei kuk).

name: Vat Phou (Wat Phu)
builtDisplay: standing structures 11th–13th c.; site from 5th c.
significance: The holy mountain of the Mekong: Lingaparvata's summit is a natural linga, and from the 5th century (pre-Angkorian Shrestapura, among the oldest Indic sites in Southeast Asia) to the Khmer empire, kings built an axial sanctuary climbing toward it, fed by a sacred spring that still bathes the (now Buddhist) shrine. UNESCO-listed in 2001 with its ancient planned landscape.
story: Local tradition remembers a yearly rite in which the mountain-god was honoured with a great buffalo offering by the Lao kings of Champasak — the Indic mountain-linga absorbed into Lao Buddhist festival, still celebrated each February full moon.

name: Pha That Luang
significance: The national symbol of Laos — a gold-covered lotus-bud stupa raised by Setthathirath when he moved the Lan Xang capital to Vientiane, on a site tradition traces to an Ashokan-era relic mission. Sacked in the 19th century and restored under the French, it centres the That Luang festival each November full moon, when the whole nation processes with wax flower-castles.
story: Five monks returning from India, the chronicle says, brought the Buddha's breastbone and enshrined it here in the 3rd century BCE under a first stupa — Laos joining its origin to Ashoka's great relic diaspora.

name: My Son Sanctuary
significance: Holy valley of the Cham kings for nine centuries — the longest continuously developed Indic sacred site in Southeast Asia, where each dynasty added brick kalan towers to Bhadresvara, the linga fusing king and god. The Chams' mortarless fired-brick technique still defies full explanation. B-52 carpet bombing in 1969 cratered the finest group; UNESCO listed the survivors in 1999.
story: Cham legend and inscription fuse founder-king Bhadravarman with Shiva as one name — Bhadresvara — the earliest royal linga cult of its kind in Southeast Asia, seeding the god-king idea Angkor would monumentalise.

name: Po Nagar Towers
deity: Yan Po Nagar (Bhagavati / Thien Y A Na)
significance: The goddess-temple of the southern Cham realm above the Cai river mouth — a 23 m brick tower to Yan Po Nagar, mother of the kingdom, identified with Bhagavati. Uniquely, worship never stopped changing hands: Vietnamese devotees today honour the same image as the goddess Thien Y A Na, incense unbroken across the transfer of civilisations.
story: Po Nagar, the Cham mother-goddess, taught the people rice and weaving; the Vietnamese retelling makes her a sandalwood spirit-girl who floated to China, wed a prince, and returned home in the fragrant log — one goddess, two peoples, one shrine.

name: Batu Caves Sri Subramaniar Temple
significance: The great Murugan shrine of the Tamil diaspora: a limestone cathedral-cave reached by 272 rainbow-painted steps beneath the world's tallest Murugan statue (42.7 m, gilded 2006). At Thaipusam over a million devotees carry kavadi burdens and milk pots up the stairs — the largest Hindu festival gathering outside South Asia.
story: Founder Thamboosamy Pillai, struck by the cave mouth's shape — the point of Murugan's vel — installed the deity in 1891; the god of Tamil hills thus claimed a Malaysian hill, and indentured-labour descendants made it their Palani across the sea.
access: 13 km north of KL; KTM Komuter Batu Caves station at the foot.

name: Sri Mahamariamman Temple, Kuala Lumpur
significance: The oldest functioning Hindu temple in Kuala Lumpur, founded 1873 by the same Thamboosamy Pillai who later opened Batu Caves — mother-goddess protector of the early Tamil migrants. Its 22.9 m five-tiered gopuram of 228 deities rises straight out of Chinatown; the temple's silver chariot leads the Thaipusam procession to Batu Caves each year.
story: Mariamman, the rain-and-smallpox mother of Tamil villages, travelled with every ship of indentured labourers as guardian against disease in strange lands — her KL house began as their first refuge of last resort.

name: Bujang Valley (Candi Bukit Batu Pahat)
significance: Malaysia's cradle of civilisation: over 50 excavated candi of the ancient Kedah kingdom on the Straits trade route, trading with Pallava India and the Srivijayan world — Sanskrit inscriptions, Shaiva shrines and Buddhist stupas together. Candi Bukit Batu Pahat, reassembled on its riverside terrace, is the emblem; the Sungai Batu digs pushed local ironworking and monuments to the early centuries CE.
story: Tamil poetics knew this coast as Kadaram, prize of the Chola overseas expeditions — Rajendra Chola's fleet struck here in 1025, the rare moment an Indian empire crossed the ocean in force, remembered on both shores.

name: Kek Lok Si Temple
significance: The largest Buddhist temple complex in Malaysia, terraced up Penang Hill around the Ban Po Thar pagoda — Chinese octagonal base, Thai middle tiers, Burmese crown: three Buddhist worlds in one tower, mirroring Penang's port cosmopolitanism. The 36.5 m bronze Kuan Yin and Lunar New Year illumination of tens of thousands of lamps are Penang institutions.
story: The founding abbot chose Air Itam's hills for their resemblance to a crane spreading wings over water — geomancy and refuge combined: 'Kek Lok' is the Pure Land, Sukhavati, promised within sight of the migrant harbour below.

name: Sri Mariamman Temple, Singapore
significance: Singapore's oldest Hindu temple, founded in 1827 by Naraina Pillai — the Penang clerk who arrived with Raffles and became the settlement's first Indian community leader. A gazetted National Monument in the heart of Chinatown; its annual Theemithi fire-walking festival, when devotees cross burning coals for Draupadi, closes the Mariamman ritual year.
story: Pillai installed the goddess first in wood and attap on land granted for the new colony's Indian temple — Mariamman guarding migrants against epidemic in the port city, as she had in every village they left behind.

name: Borobudur
significance: The largest Buddhist monument in the world: a stone mandala-mountain of nine terraces, 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddhas, walking pilgrims from the world of desire through the world of forms to the formless summit stupa. Abandoned as Java turned to Islam, buried in ash, cleared under Raffles in 1814, and saved by the great UNESCO restoration of 1975–83; Vesak at Borobudur remains Indonesian Buddhism's central rite.
story: Javanese tradition names the divine architect Gunadharma, whose profile is traced in the Menoreh hills that watch the monument; the hidden 'Karmawibhangga' reliefs of cause and effect lie deliberately buried at the base — the law of karma literally underlying the whole mountain.
access: ~40 km from Yogyakarta; timed summit tickets via Borobudur Park.

name: Prambanan (Candi Rara Jonggrang)
significance: The greatest Hindu temple of Indonesia and Borobudur's counterpart across the plain — 240 shrines originally, the 47 m Shiva tower flanked by Brahma and Vishnu, ringed with Ramayana reliefs that the Ramayana Ballet still dances against the floodlit towers on full-moon nights. Raised by Rakai Pikatan as the Hindu answer of the Sanjaya line to the Sailendras' Borobudur; UNESCO-listed in 1991.
story: Prince Bandung Bondowoso, to win Rara Jonggrang, had to build a thousand temples in one night; when spirits neared success she had the village women pound rice to trick the cocks into crowing dawn. Enraged at 999, he cursed her to stone — the slender Durga in the north cell, the 'slender maiden' the complex is named for.

name: Pura Besakih (Mother Temple)
builtDisplay: complex grown over 700+ years; origins older
originNote: Attributed to Rsi Markandeya's mission to Bali
significance: The Mother Temple of Bali: 23 linked puras on Mount Agung's slope, axis of the island's mandala of temples, where every Balinese clan and kingdom keeps a shrine. The Eka Dasa Rudra — the once-a-century purification of the universe — was underway in 1963 when Agung erupted catastrophically; lava spared the temple by metres, read across Bali as the gods' own testimony.
story: The sage Markandeya, guided by a vision, buried the panca datu — five sacred metals — here to still the island's unquiet forces; on that buried offering the whole thousand-year edifice of Balinese Hinduism literally stands.

name: Pura Tanah Lot
significance: Bali's sea-rock icon: one of the chain of sea temples ringing the island's coast, each within sight of the next, established in the wanderings of the Javanese priest Nirartha as Majapahit's Hindu high culture took final refuge in Bali. Cut off at high tide, silhouetted at sunset, it is among the most photographed sacred sites in Asia; a third of the rock was quietly rebuilt in a 1980s Japanese-aided restoration.
story: Nirartha, resting on the rock, was challenged by the local priest; he meditated the rock loose from the land, set his sash upon the waves as sea snakes to guard it, and left them there — the striped kraits in the base caves are honoured as those guardians still.

name: Pura Luhur Uluwatu
significance: One of Bali's six sad kahyangan directional temples, on a 70 m sea cliff at the island's southwestern point — guarding Bali from the spirits of the ocean as the sun goes down. The kecak fire-dance performed at its clifftop amphitheatre each sunset, chanting the Ramayana's monkey army, is the island's signature ritual-theatre.
story: Here Nirartha ended his earthly wanderings, attaining moksha in a flash of light from the cliff — 'Ulu-watu', the headland's stone, holding the point where the priest of all Bali's sea temples left the world; the temple monkeys are held to guard his relics with famous mischief.

name: Dieng Plateau Temples (Arjuna group)
significance: The oldest surviving temples of Java, small stone candi standing in a volcanic caldera 2,000 m up — 'Di Hyang', abode of the gods, where Indian temple form first took Javanese root a century before Borobudur. Of perhaps 400 original shrines, eight remain among sulphur vents and coloured lakes, named by later tradition for wayang heroes: Arjuna, Bima, Gatotkaca, Srikandi.
story: Mist rolling over the caldera gave rise to the belief that this is where gods and ancestors meet; the annual ruwatan here shaves the dreadlocked 'gimbal' children of the plateau, releasing them from spirit-claims in a rite that predates and outlived the temples' own worship.
